### Both policies answer the same question: when a CPU writes to an address that’s in the cache, when does main memory find out?

### Write-through ensures memory is always consistent with the cache

On every write, the cache updates its own copy and immediately writes the value to the next level (memory or a lower cache). Memory is always consistent with the cache.

Pros: Simple. Memory is never stale, so cache coherence in multiprocessor systems is easier, and a cache line can be dropped on eviction without writing anything back. Crash recovery is easier because memory holds the latest data.

Cons: Every store generates memory traffic, so write bandwidth and latency become a bottleneck. This is usually softened with a write buffer, which lets the CPU continue while writes drain in the background, but the buffer can still fill under heavy write bursts.

### Write-back delays memory updates until a dirty line is evicted

On a write hit, the cache updates only its own copy and sets a dirty bit on that line. Memory is updated later, when the dirty line is evicted (or flushed explicitly).

Pros: Repeated writes to the same line collapse into a single memory write, which saves a lot of bandwidth and power. Writes complete at cache speed. It also lets you write whole lines in bursts, which memory handles efficiently.

Cons: More complex. You need dirty bits and eviction logic, and evicting a dirty line costs an extra write that can add latency on a miss. Memory can hold stale data, so multiprocessor systems need a coherence protocol (MESI and similar) to make sure other cores and DMA devices see the right values. A crash or power loss can lose data that was only in the cache.

### Write misses determine whether a line is loaded on a write

Each policy is usually paired with a write-miss policy:

1. Write-allocate loads the line into the cache, then performs the write. This is typically paired with write-back, since later writes to nearby data will then hit.
2. No-write-allocate sends the write straight to memory without loading the line. This is typically paired with write-through, since there’s little benefit in caching data you only wrote.

### Comparison of write policies

| | Write-through | Write-back |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Memory traffic | High (every write) | Low (on eviction) |
| Memory consistency | Always up to date | Can be stale |
| Complexity | Low | Higher (dirty bits, coherence) |
| Eviction cost | None | Extra write if dirty |
| Data-loss risk on crash | Low | Higher |

### Write-back dominates in modern CPU caches while write-through serves specific durability needs

In practice: Write-back dominates in modern CPU caches (L1 through L3) because bandwidth and speed matter most. Write-through shows up where consistency and simplicity matter more, such as some L1 designs (often paired with a write-back L2 behind them), embedded systems, and storage or database layers that need durability guarantees. The same tradeoff appears outside hardware too: OS page caches and disk controllers use write-back for speed, while “write-through” modes are offered when you can’t afford to lose recent writes.

analysis.main_topic: Write-through and write-back cache write policies and their tradeoffs
primary_claims: Write-through updates both the cache and the next level of memory immediately on every write, ensuring memory is always consistent.
Write-through simplifies crash recovery and cache coherence but creates a bottleneck in write bandwidth and latency.
Write-back updates only the cache on a write hit, setting a dirty bit, and updates memory only when the line is evicted.
Write-back saves bandwidth and power by collapsing repeated writes, but introduces complexity requiring dirty bits, eviction logic, and coherence protocols.
Write-allocate is typically paired with write-back, while no-write-allocate is typically paired with write-through.
existing_examples: Modern CPU caches (L1 through L3) using write-back
Some L1 designs paired with a write-back L2
Embedded systems and storage or database layers using write-through
OS page caches and disk controllers using write-back
missing_intermediate_steps: Detailed mechanics of how a write buffer drains into main memory
Step-by-step state transitions of a cache coherence protocol like MESI
assumed_prior_knowledge: How CPU reads and writes interact with memory hierarchies
Basic understanding of hardware crashes and data persistence
possible_confusions: Confusing when main memory is updated versus when the cache is updated
Confusing write policies with write-miss policies (write-allocate vs no-write-allocate)

learning_objectives: Understand the mechanism of write-through caching and its tradeoffs
Understand the mechanism of write-back caching and its tradeoffs
Distinguish between write-allocate and no-write-allocate cache policies
explanation_sequence: Define the core problem of when main memory is updated on a write
Explain write-through policy, its pros, cons, and write buffer usage
Explain write-back policy, its pros, cons, and dirty bits
Explain write misses and the pairing with write-allocate and no-write-allocate
Compare summary metrics and real-world applications

preserved_claims: Write-through writes to the cache and the backing store before the write is considered complete.
Write-back writes to the cache first and copies the changed data to backing storage later.
Write-back can lose unflushed changes if the cache fails before writing back; write-through writes to backing storage more immediately.
Write-back usually has faster write performance because it delays the slower backing-store writes.
